claim: Bill Gates said of software piracy in China: 'as long as they're going to steal it, we want them to steal ours. They'll get sort of addicted, and then we'll somehow figure out how to collect sometime in the next decade.' (B4)
source: Schlender (1998), Fortune, 20 July 1998; read via Wayback snapshot 2025-03-06 of money.cnn.com fortune_archive/1998/07/20/245683/index.htm
evidence: Wording matches the article exactly. Context (Gates answering a question about the 1995 China trip): 'Although about three million computers get sold every year in China, people don't pay for the software. Someday they will, though. And as long as they're going to steal it, we want them to steal ours. They'll get sort of addicted, and then we'll somehow figure out how to collect sometime in the next decade.' Event: University of Washington, Seattle, a Friday in late May 1998; article is an edited Q&A, byline 'By Brent Schlender; Warren Buffett; Bill Gates'.
corrected_reference_apa7: Schlender, B. (1998, July 20). The Bill & Warren show. *Fortune*. https://money.cnn.com/magazines/fortune/fortune_archive/1998/07/20/245683/index.htm
notes: Proposed excerpt (14 words, verbatim): "They'll get sort of addicted, and then we'll somehow figure out how to collect". Alternative (14 words): "as long as they're going to steal it, we want them to steal ours". Use one only (one-quote rule). The remark is about China in 1998; attribute as Gates quoted in Schlender (1998). Author's URL lacks index.htm; live page returned HTTP 503 / 404 page on 2026-10-22, so cite the index.htm URL and keep the archive link in the log. It does not show that vendors deliberately seed cracked copies; it supports only tolerating piracy to build dependence.

claim: Conner & Rumelt (1991): with network effects, leaving software unprotected can raise profits (B4)
source: Crossref record and published abstract, doi 10.1287/mnsc.37.2.125
evidence: Abstract: 'in some circumstances, even with significant piracy, not protecting can be the best policy, both raising firm profits and lowering selling prices. Key to the analysis is joining the presence of a positive network externality with the fact that piracy increases the total number of program users.' The externality comes from users economizing on post-purchase learning and customization costs. Crossref: Management Science 37(2), 125-139, February 1991; authors Kathleen Reavis Conner, Richard P. Rumelt.
corrected_reference_apa7: Conner, K. R., & Rumelt, R. P. (1991). Software piracy: An analysis of protection strategies. *Management Science, 37*(2), 125–139. https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.37.2.125
notes: Full text not read (INFORMS paywall); claim matches the abstract. Say 'in some circumstances' rather than as a general rule.

claim: Givon, Mahajan & Muller (1995): most users had pirated copies, yet pirates drove most new legal adopters by word of mouth (B4)
source: Crossref record with published abstract (doi 10.1177/002224299505900103); copyrightevidence.org summary; Waters (2013) MPRA 46036
evidence: Abstract: applied to spreadsheets and word processors in the United Kingdom; 'although six of every seven software users utilized pirated copies, these pirates were responsible for generating more than 80% of new software buyers'. Data period (secondary: copyrightevidence.org and Waters 2013): monthly UK shipment data, January 1987 to August 1992 (68 periods), DOS-based software.
corrected_reference_apa7: Givon, M., Mahajan, V., & Muller, E. (1995). Software piracy: Estimation of lost sales and the impact on software diffusion. *Journal of Marketing, 59*(1), 29–37. https://doi.org/10.1177/002224299505900103
notes: Use the DOI rather than the JSTOR URL. These are model estimates: piracy was not observed (Waters 2013: 'we have no piracy data') but inferred from a diffusion model. Waters (2013) found that for word processors, under one error specification, piracy only displaced legal sales. Suggested wording: 'A 1995 model of UK spreadsheet and word-processor sales (1987-1992) estimated that six of seven users had pirated copies, yet pirates brought in more than 80% of new buyers.' 'Word of mouth' is a fair gloss of 'influence potential software users'. Full text not read (SAGE and JSTOR blocked).

claim: Peitz & Waelbroeck (2006): review of the theoretical piracy literature that includes the network-effect argument (B4)
